newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo plans 1,200 km in new highways by 2001.
newsitem.headline: Yugo plans 1,200 km in new highways by 2001.

text.p: Yugoslavia plans to create a modern trans-Yugoslav highway network by adding around 1,200 kilometres of new roads by 2001, creating a shorter road link between Europe and the Middle East.
Trans-Yugoslav highways would employ at least 15,000 construction workers and give a boost to the economy, Serbia's Transportation Minister Svetolik Kostadinovic said on Tuesday.
Highway links between north and south of Yugoslavia are seen geographically as the shortest way between Europe and Greece, Bulgaria, Turkey and Middle East.
The government planned to build six stretches within the five-year project, creating quicker links between its borders, Kostadinovic told Reuters in an interview.
Works on the first 71-km stretch between Horgos, at the Yugoslav-Hungarian border, and Feketic in northern Serbia, will commence on Sunday, the minister said.
The Horgos-Feketic toll-road will become fully operational by the end of 1997 and is expected to bring around 15 million German marks in earnings in 1998, Kostadinovic said.
Money will be invested in new road projects.
"The government also plans for this year to start building a 37-km ring road around Belgrade and divert traffic from the capital," Kostadinovic said.
Other plans included Leskovac-Macedonian border, Belgrade-Cacak-South Adriatic coast, Nis-Pristina-Pec-Cakor and Nis-Dimitrovgrad stretches, the minister said.
The government currently generates funds for road-building by collecting a special 0.5 dinar tax from 3.75 dinars for each litre of petrol sold.
"This is a stable source of financing and is used exclusively for the trans-Yugoslav highways project," Kostadinovic said.
The tax could bring the state around one billion dinars ($178 million) in 1997.
But Serbia was also readying a new concessions law to attract foreign investment in big infrastructure projects.
The Construction Ministry has prepared a new law on concessions to be adopted in the parliament in April at the latest.
The law sets criteria and conditions for getting concessions for road building, equally for foreign and domestic companies, the minister said.

"The government has also set up a special commission of representatives from the ministries of construction, finance and transportation, charged with preparing (international) tenders and choosing bidders," Kostadinovic said.
As soon as the law is adopted, the commission will call tenders and the best bidders will be chosen by the end of 1997, the minister added.

Foreigners can opt for a simple concession deal, create joint ventures with local companies or enter a deal with the government on an investment- and profit-sharing basis. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
